extracted.intended_audience: natural philosophers / educated readers interested in early-modern physics, meteorology, and natural theology
extracted.subtask_description: A chapter-length exposition (early modern) giving experimental observations and theoretical principles about air, fire, vapours, buoyancy, precipitation, and the rôle of mountains in collecting moisture. Intended to show how experiments and hydrostatics explain meteorological phenomena.

rubrics_metrics.name: Air adheres to other matters
rubrics_metrics.description: Experiments show that the Air does likewise adhere to other Matters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence: rusty nails in clear water show little air-bubbles cleaving to them; pieces of rusty iron and brass thrown into lye (which 'has no Air') form bubbles that expand under exhaustion and prove to be Air. Conclusion/implication: air will cleave to solid bodies and even to metals (may be cause of rusting).

rubrics_metrics.name: Fire cleaves to solid bodies
rubrics_metrics.description: Fire can stick to heavier and solid Bodies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence and citation: red-hot flint and other refractory bodies retain heat attributable to adhering fire-particles rather than mere swift motion of parts. Boyle's experiments (de ponderabil. part. flamma) show copper, tin, steel, silver, pewter, burnt hartshorn, chalk and coral become heavier by particles of fire that cleave to them. Additional proof: some bodies enclosed in glass increased weight only by pure flames of brimstone or spirit of wine, implying small fire particles penetrate pores of glass.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fire adheres to water (fire-water adhesion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Fire can join itself to Water; the heat/particles of fire adhere to water and can be released under reduced pressure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Air-pump experiments: a glass or teacup of very hot water under a receiver often shows, upon exhaustion, violent motion (like boiling) and ejection; cold water under the same conditions discloses only a few bubbles. Lye (no air) under exhaustion bursts out by expansion attributable to particles of fire contained in it. Observations: water taken out after such motion is colder to the touch than water never under the receiver, indicating loss of 'fire-particles'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fire should be esteemed a particular substance
rubrics_metrics.description: From experiments it seems reasonable to conclude that Fire is a particular Substance, not merely a swift motion of parts of other bodies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument: waters become colder after motion under exhaustion (due to removal of fire-particles), and hot water under receiver shows different behaviour from cold water; such phenomena suggest fire has independent particulate reality rather than being merely motion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fire-particles are elastic and expansive
rubrics_metrics.description: Fire-particles display elasticity and expansiveness when freed from the pressure of the air.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observation: by removing the pressure of the air that keeps them down, fire-particles exert their own motion and expand — a property akin to elasticity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fire departs from water when air is thinner
rubrics_metrics.description: Fire which sticks close to water abandons the water and flies away when it comes into an Air which is thinner (less pressure).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequent phenomenon: when vapours are raised into thinner air, the adhering fire separates and rises, leaving the water more apt to condense and fall as precipitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fire + Water can form a composition lighter than air
rubrics_metrics.description: Fire and Water united and mingled together may make a Composition lighter than so much Air, and which can ascend in it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogous examples: iron and cork fastened together float upon water though iron alone sinks; lumps of brimstone in lye produce bubbles that drive bits upward; volatile salts and burning spirits ascend by small heat. Implication: small heat (some fire) can make water evaporate and rise even without full boiling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaporation requires division into very small particles
rubrics_metrics.description: Water must be divided into exceeding small particles in order to be evaporated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence: distillations and chemical sublimations produce fine particles rather than large drops; smoke (minute particles) rises carried by adhering fire, but larger soot collects and will not ascend until reduced to smaller size. Thus particle size is crucial to the ability to be carried upward.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vapours ascend by thermal effects (heat and cold effects)
rubrics_metrics.description: Water being heated (by sun or fires) will be carried up into the air; moreover vapours are observed to ascend from low grounds in cold weather and ice/snow can be lighter than their liquid water.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observation: vapours arise from warm sources; yet vapours also emerge in the cold (low grounds in cold weather), and ice/snow are lighter than the water of which they are composed, implying ascent/evaporation phenomena relate to both thermal extremes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law I of Hydrostatics (buoyancy criterion for ascent)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a Body is to be carried upwards in any Liquor, an equal Bulk of the said Liquor must gravitate or weigh more than such a Body.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statement of hydrostatical principle used to explain why objects or vapour compositions float — equal volume of surrounding fluid must weigh more than the body for upward motion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law II of Hydrostatics (buoyancy criterion for sinking)
rubrics_metrics.description: In order to cause a Body to sink in a Liquor, an equal Bulk of the said Liquor must weigh less than the Body.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Complementary hydrostatic law: sinking occurs when the body is heavier than an equal volume of the surrounding fluid.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law III of Hydrostatics (neutral equilibrium)
rubrics_metrics.description: If you would have the Body neither to rise nor fall, but preserve its Place in any Part of the Liquor, an equal Quantity of the said Liquor must weigh equally with the Body.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Neutral buoyancy: equal weights (body vs equal bulk of fluid) produce suspension at a given depth; used to explain clouds remaining pendulous at an equilibrium level.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vapours adapt to hydrostatical equilibrium levels
rubrics_metrics.description: Vapours rise until they reach a region of the air where the surrounding air's gravity/density equals that of the vapour (their equilibrium), and there they float as clouds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Model: the atmosphere grows finer upwards; vapours ascend to the bound of equilibrium (F GH), float like clouds where equipois'd, and descend if raised into even thinner air where they become too heavy relative to that layer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sun/fire adhesion makes vapours able to float as clouds
rubrics_metrics.description: Waters united to the Sun-Beams or Fire form vapours that are raised into the air and float as clouds according to hydrostatical laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mechanism: union with fire (heat, sun-beams) makes a composition lighter than air; experimental demonstrations with air-pump and examples of high-flying mists and clouds are given.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vapours descend by collision and compression (coalescence)
rubrics_metrics.description: When opposing winds drive mists or clouds against each other they are collected into drops, becoming heavier than an equal quantity of air and will fall down.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: distillations where vapours are compressed in a narrow neck and run into watery drops; macroscopic weather process where converging winds provoke formation of rain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vapours descend by separation of fire-particles on entering thinner air
rubrics_metrics.description: If a cloud is driven into a higher, thinner air, the fire-particles that made it lighter extricate themselves and ascend, so the water becomes too heavy and falls as dew, mist, rain, snow, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experimentally supported by air-pump tests: moving vapour to regions of different pressure causes separation of adhering fire and subsequent precipitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Air rarefaction (air becoming lighter) causes vapour descent
rubrics_metrics.description: When the air becomes thinner/lighter (for various reasons), vapours that were previously supported may descend, as evidenced experimentally and by barometer readings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proofs: glass air-pump experiments, barometer (mercury falls on the least weight of the air prognosticating fogs, vapours or rain).

rubrics_metrics.name: Cold can produce precipitation by enabling vapours to condense
rubrics_metrics.description: Sudden cessation of warmth (cold) gives opportunity to vapours to be precipitated and turned into rain; analogous to distillation 'worms' and crystallization where salts coagulate on cooling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acknowledgement of incomplete knowledge of the nature of cold, but experimental analogues in chemistry and distillation show coagulation/subsidence upon cooling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transport/motion of vapours is necessary for distribution of rainfall
rubrics_metrics.description: The motion of vapours (winds) is necessary so that vapours raised in one place may fall in another; without transport local exhalations would only return to their source and provide little advantage elsewhere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implications: distribution of rivers, fertility of distant lands, and the quenching of thirst in arid regions depend on winds carrying clouds. Thought experiments about islands and deserts illustrate need for transport.

rubrics_metrics.name: Watry vapours leave their salts behind (desalination by evaporation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Most vapours exhaled from the sea leave salts behind, yielding fresh water upon condensation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence: distillation/sublimation and salt-works show salt remains at the bottom while vapours condense as fresh water; explains why dew, rain and snow are fresh despite originating from salt sea.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mountains collect vapours and produce local clouds
rubrics_metrics.description: Mountains serve to collect the vapours in the air and are frequently covered with thick clouds, producing streams and abundant rains on their slopes even in hot zones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observational testimony: accounts of St. Thomas, Madagascar, Teneriffe, Varenius and travellers; mountains frequently have clouds at their summits and provide streams and rivers from collected dew and vapours.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mountains furnish springs and rivers by condensing collected vapours
rubrics_metrics.description: One of the chief uses of mountains is to collect the vapours and turn them into fountains, springs, brooks and lastly rivers, transmitting water from their heights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument and cited dissertation (Dr. Halley) based on experience (e.g., St. Helena observations). Implication: mountains are essential to the hydrological cycle and the supply of fresh water to continents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regular hydrostatic and meteorological order suggests wise design
rubrics_metrics.description: The conformity of vapour ascent/descent and hydrostatical rules, and the usefulness of mountains and winds to distribute water, provide grounds for concluding an intelligent direction rather than mere chance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rhetorical/theological inference: the precise and beneficial operation of these natural processes (cloud formation, rain, rivers) argues for the wisdom/goodness of the Creator; presented as a conclusion for the reader to consider.
